speechtext:

Returns are also received in the department which reveal, as of the last day of each

month, the percentage of unemployment among the recognized trades, who are members of trade unions. This magazine is published in New York city. So far as the Post Office Department is concerned, at one time this magazine did have what is known as the mailing in Canada privilege. It does not enjoy that privilege to-day, which would indicate that it would have to come into Canada by either freight or express. Was the tender of E. G. M. Cape and Company accepted and at what figure?

question:	At what figure was the tender

maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS
subtopic: MONTREAL TERMINAL-REFERENCE TO ANSWER GIVEN THIS DAY TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: I may say that I have followed the practice, which I think has been in vogue for many years, that of referring questions concerning the operation of the Canadian National railways to the railway management and filing in this house such information as is received from the management. maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS
subtopic: MONTREAL TERMINAL-REFERENCE TO ANSWER GIVEN THIS DAY TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Once again, on a question of the privilege of the house, I think it ought to be made perfectly clear to the minister that if reasonable information is not given in the way I have suggested, it forces those of us who are seeking that information, when the committee is appointed or on the estimates, to enter into a more or less controversial discussion or attack in order to extract the information. maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES

speechtext:
The house resumed from Friday, February 10, consideration in committee of the following proposed resolution-Mr. Dunning-Mr. Sanderson in the chair:
That the governor in council be authorized to raise by way of loan under the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, 1931, an amount not to exceed in the whole the sum of seven hundred and fifty million dollars for paying or redeeming the whole or any portion of loans or obligations of Canada, and also for purchasing and withdrawing from circulation unmatured securities of Canada, and for public works and general purposes.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance): Mr. Chairman, I believe the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Landeryou) had the floor.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: I should like to ask the Minister of Finance a question. Would the carrying out of the financial operations indicated by this resolution result in a reduction or an increase in Canada's national debt?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: That is a difficult question to answer. It depends on the extent to which this house votes money for expenditures which, during the period covered, cannot be met out of the current revenues of the country. To that extent the debt of the country may be increased. With regard to the refunding operations, with which the bill is mainly designed to deal, no increase in public debt will be involved.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Does the government intend to set aside any reserve to retire this debt within a period of twenty years?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
I believe I have indicated on a number of occasions my own belief that a sinking fund policy is a desirable one for Canada, and that as soon as the finances of the country reach such a condition that an annual provision for sinking fund against the national debt can be instituted, I personally would favour such a course. I do not think it would be a good thing to get into the position in which other countries having definite sinking fund provisions have found themselves during the past few years. For instance, in Great Britain it has been all too common in recent years for the chancellor of the exchequer, on account of prevailing conditions, to be compelled to ask in his budget for the suspension of the sinking

Loan of $750,000,000
fund provisions for the current year. In the present state of dominion government revenues and expenditures in Canada, it is fairly evident that we should be likely to reach that position if we had in effect a definite sinking fund provision with respect to the whole of our debt.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: I have raised that question because I understood that in sound financing it was a cardinal principle that money be set aside in a sinking fund to take care of debt.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: In principle I agree.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: In one of the resolutions I notice it is the intention of the government to provide a sinking fund to retire in ten years the sums borrowed for capital expenditures in the Department of National Defence. I had hoped the government would possibly set aside a sinking fund to provide for the retirement of this $750,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: We are making a beginning on the principle in the manner the hon. member has indicated.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
I am pleased to note that. Section 91 of the British North America Act reads, in part, as follows:
4. The borrowing of money on the public credit.
Would the minister explain just what we mean by "public credit"?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: When the government of Canada borrows money it pledges the word of the people of Canada, as represented by their duly constituted government, to repay the amount borrowed. The public credit of Canada therefore consists of the obligation which I have just stated, authorized by this parliament.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Could the minister tell the committee just what stands behind the bonds and securities issued against the public credit? Is it just the word of the dominion, or what is it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: In the last analysis, the good faith of the people of Canada, their willingness as a people to honour their given word.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Would it be fair to say that the natural resources of Canada stand behind the bonds and securities issued by this government?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
That is a highly theoretical question. No securities issued by this dominion constitute a mortgage upon any of the business assets of the dominion. What
is given is the word of the people to pay. As I understand it, it is the word of the people that stands behind the bonded obligations of this country.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: I am glad to know that it is just the word of the people to pay. At the moment would the minister consider amending the act to provide a sinking fund?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: I have already dealt with that.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: I should like to ask a question founded on the last five words in the resolution, "public works and general purposes." Will the financing of the new station at Montreal be charged up to this program, or will it be charged to income?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: In so far as any Canadian National expenditure is an expenditure by the railway, it will of course be chargeable to the railway and not to this legislation. To the extent to which any part of the work may be a relief project, and therefore chargeable against the general revenues of the country, it would be charged here to the extent to which it may be necessary to borrow to meet that or other obligations.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
The latter part of the resolution reads:

for paying or redeeming the whole or any portion of loans or obligations of Canada, and also for purchasing and withdrawing from circulation unmatured securities of Canada.
Some of these have been sold privately and many investors have suffered losses of from one to three thousand dollars because of bond payments having to be made in Canadian funds. Will any consideration be given in the new financing to regulate or prevent in the future such losses by reason of exchange differences between New York and Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend misunderstands the intent of the words in the resolution to which he has referred. They enable the government to take advantage of the call privilege where it exists in bonds now outstanding. We have a number of issues of bonds in connection with which the government has the right to call after a certain date and at a certain price. That is why those words are in the resolution.
With respect to the question as to losses because of exchange movements, let me say to my hon. friend that any person who buys a bond of the Dominion of Canada can depend upon that bond being paid to him in the terms of the currency called for by the bond itself. That is to say, if a person is the owner of a bond of the Dominion of Canada which is payable in lawful money of the United States,
Loan of $750,000,000

it will be paid in that money regardless of what the rate of exchange may be. If he holds a bond payable in sterling in London, England, he will receive payment in the currency called for by the bond. Similarly, if he is entitled to Canadian funds, that is exactly what he will get.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Sometimes it is optional.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Yes, there are some bonds that are optional. Certain bonds guarantee payment in terms of United States or sterling currency. I am strongly opposed to issuing that kind of bond, and I do not think it is likely that any more will be issued. The volume of these bonds is being reduced gradually by maturities and by call, but in such cases the Canadian government, in accordance with the terms of the bond, must pay the holder thereof in the currency he chooses to receive. He has the option -of being paid in either one of two currencies.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
This resolution
says, "and for public works and general purposes." Can the minister tell us how much of this money is to be used for public works and general purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: I shall try that again. This is not a spending authority, this is a borrowing authority. The extent to which this will be used to cover expenditures will be determined, not by this legislation but by the amounts voted from time to time by this house in relation to the total revenues received by the dominion. If this house votes an aggregate sum of money going beyond the total revenues of the dominion, then the balance must be borrowed. Similarly, certain expenditures are stated in the estimates to be capital expenditures, against which money is borrowed. It is intended to give to the Department of Finance authority to borrow such moneys as this house from time to time determines shall be raised for the purposes indicated.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Should not parliament be told how much money is to be spent on public works and for other purposes before this measure is passed? There does not seem to me to be any great rush about giving the government power to borrow this money before parliament knows for what it is to be borrowed. I am heartily in accord with the principle of borrowing money for refunding and such purposes, but before we give authority for the borrowing we have a right to know for what purpose the money is being borrowed, especially in the light of conditions as we have them to-day, with the terrible taxes and tremendous debt facing this country.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
I indicated some days
ago that I would ask the minister to be good enough to break down this resolution and give us certain information, which would include the information asked for by my hon. friend. If the committee will permit I should like to ask the minister to reply to three or four questions I shall ask along that line.
The resolution states that this money is for paying or redeeming the whole or any portion of loans or obligations of Canada. Will the minister state what loans or obligations are covered by that particular part of the resolution? I have before me the public accounts, which as near as I can judge show that something in the neighbourhood of $425,000,000 will mature in 1939 and 1940. I understand that this resolution is intended to cover 1940. I should like the minister to give us a list of the maturing obligations which it is intended to retire by this resolution. I shall then follow up with one or two other questions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: My hon. friend has had experience as a minister of the crown, and I am sure he knows well the answer to his own question.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: He knows that this is not a spending authority but a borrowing authority. My hon. friend knows that I cannot possibly tell him the answer to his question. No one ever could, and in my experience this is the first time that an effort has been made to involve the question of the general borrowing authority with that of the spending authority, which is otherwise provided for by this parliament. I am sure my hon. friend knows that there is no means of answering his question.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: I will tell the minister just why I am exhibiting this high degree of ignorance.	[DOT]

speechtext: I am informed, and I think I am not very far out, that the government has in preparation a large public works program amounting to something in the neighbourhood of $100,000,000. I understand that the amount at present before the government is some $112,000,000.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: We will let that pass. It is true that the minister, as the watch dog of the treasury, will probably sift that down considerably, but what I am concerned about is this: If we give the minister this authority to borrow for public works and general purposes, and he has there a sum amounting to about $175,000,000 which may be used for those purposes, I think we are entitled to know what the special supplementary estimates are going to be before the bill founded on this resolution is passed-either that or the minister should state clearly what proportion of this amount will be used for these purposes. The minister, of course is in an advantageous position. He can laugh at me; he can make light of it, because perhaps a month or two will pass before these very luscious supplementary estimates are brought down. But I have been here long enough to know that in a session preceding an anticipated election, usually a very fine, fat, supplementary public works estimate is brought down. I am not particularly objecting to that provided that the public works estimates this year are directed towards the relief of unemployment. What I do and shall object to is the voting of huge sums of money to be distributed among the constituencies of Canada in a manner best calculated to bring the greatest possible influence to bear upon the electorate in favour of the government. That is what I object to, and that is why I think we are entitled to a clear statement as to what proportion of this authorization will be available for those purposes. The minister is very fair and very courteous, and I compliment him in that regard. But all we know is that the $575,000,000 is clearly provided for, except that of the $155,000,000 of treasury bills, I imagine that at least $100,000,000 will be renewed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Yes, but from my experience I would say that at least $100,000,000 will be renewed, which means that only $475,000,000 out of this $750,000,000 is actually allocated. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES

-obviously interested in

It happens that I am
referring to the 175 supporters of the government in the house. However, that does not alter my opinion that we are entitled this afternoon to a definite statement as to what proportion of this huge sum of $750,000,000 may reasonably be expected to be used for the purposes I have mentioned. I will venture to say, from my experience of twenty-eight years in this house, that during that period estimates have not been changed more than half a dozen times. I doubt if it is half a dozen. maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES

I am very glad to hear that, but I should like to see them down before this resolution passes, so that we can have a look at them. However, I repeat that when that supplementary comes down it will pass as a matter of course.
The minister talks about appropriations. Of course these appropriations are made by parliament; but, as I said a moment ago, they are made by the government, supported by their followers in the house, and they pass as a matter of course.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES

borrowing.

speechtext: If I were in the minister's place I would increase the financing of this country by treasury bills. That is one thing. And I would go further. If the minister accepted my advice he would endeavour in this period of stress, provided he had a policy that would tend to the permanent relief of this unemployment question-which the government now have not-

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES

The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie), a colleague of my hon. friend the Minister of

words Australia is very similar to Canada in regard to the amount of currency in circulation.
There is one explanation as to why we have less currency in circulation in this country than they have in the United States. There is a different explanation with respect to Great Britain. The explanation with regard to the United States is one with which every hon. member of this house who thinks is familiar. The Canadian public have a great deal more confidence in their banking system than the people of the United States have in the banking system of that country. The hoarding of actual currency in the United States is known and acknowledged by the United States authorities to be very large indeed, whereas' the deserved and continued confidence of the Canadian people in the Canadian banking system has involved an ever-increasing growth in the use of checking accounts instead of piling up large volumes of currency.
With respect to Great Britain, for a different set of reasons altogether the British people have not come along in the use of checking accounts to anything like the extent to which that method has been used in this country. Just here I should like to quote from the December bulletin of the United States federal reserve system touching on this exact point in connection with the volume of currency in circulation in that country. This bulletin is authoritative; as hon. members know, the federal reserve system is a governmental institution in that country. The bulletin states:
The higher level of currency in circulation that has been maintained since 1936 at about $2,000,000,000 above that of 1929 represents increases both in large-denomination currency and in coin and small-denomination bills. The increase in large bills reflects in part the holding of savings in the form of currency rather than in bank deposits, securities, or other property. The banking difficulties in the early thirties may be partly responsible for the increase in the volume of savings held in currency rather than in banks, notwithstanding the safeguarding of bank deposits after 1933 by federal deposit insurance. Another factor is probably the reduction in interest rates paid on savings and other time deposits.
I would direct attention to the fact that the $2,000,000,000 there noted as the increase in United States circulation since 1936 would account for approximately $16 per capita of the difference between that country's per capita circulation of currency and the circulation of currency in Canada.
I do not know that there is anything I Gan add to what has been said already, except this one point which I overlooked. I was asked the other day as to the proportion of
Canada's funded debt which was held in Canada and the proportion payable in other countries. I have the figure here somewhere and will be glad to place it on record. Without waiting to find that figure I would say that as things stand at present, seventy-five per cent of the funded debt of Canada is due and payable to Canadian people in Canada. That, I think, is a record of which we have no reason to be ashamed.
There is just one other point bearing on the same question. The other day the hon. member for Kootenay East asked us to give consideration to whether or not Canadians should increase their indebtedness to the United States. At that time I indicated to him that all the matters to which he referred were of necessity receiving constant study at the hands of the experts of the finance department, the officers of the central bank and, necessarily, myself. I can tell him now that the latest information with respect to the movement in that regard, developed by the bureau of statistics, indicated that there has been a net reduction of Canada's indebtedness abroad-I am speaking now not of the government alone but of all indebtedness abroad by all Canadians-of $524,000,000 during the past five years.
I indicated to my hon. friend, who expressed some doubt the other day, that I was quite sure that there had been during the last few years a continuous reduction in the balance of indebtedness in foreign countries against the Canadian people. This is the figure vouched for by the bureau of statistics in that regard: $524,800,000, in the last five years.

I will answer him at once and say that this government does not believe, under the conditions now prevailing, or under the conditions which have prevailed since we came into office, in tying the Canadian dollar to any other currency anywhere, whether it be the pound sterling or the American dollar. I would earnestly submit to this committee that the moment we do so we abdicate the function with which the Canadian people have entrusted us, namely that of managing our own currency. We cease to manage it ourselves the moment we tie it up to any other currency. At the present time the Canadian dollar rides on the tide of trade. It is not tied to any other currency, and I 
think any student of present conditions would question the desirability of tying it either to the United States dollar on the one hand or to the pound sterling on the other.
My hon. friend painted an alluring picture of the benefits to be derived from tying our dollar to a depreciated pound. He spoke, as many do, of the advantages to certain groups of producers, and of the disadvantage to those having securities payable in terms of United States currency. He did not mention at all the effect it would have upon all the people of Canada who are consumers. He did not mention at all the fact that depreciating our currency in relation to the United States dollar at this minute would impose a protective tariff much more effective than anything we have. To the extent of the difference between the depreciated Canadian dollar and the United States dollar it would impose a tariff against all imports entering this country, without, in so doing, bringing in a cent of revenue to the Canadian treasury, but definitely increasing the cost of all domestic commodities which have to be purchased which are governed by the cost of imported commodities. The thing is not so easy as that. If it were, does anybody suppose that any government would not desire to get additional returns for primary producers of exportable products? Would it not be something that we would jump at? My hon. friend well knows that it is much more complicated in its essence than that. In my best judgment, advising the government on these matters, with conditions as they are to-day, it would be definitely bad business for the Canadian people to have their dollar tied to any other country's currency. In the changing circumstances which surround us today we must retain control of our own currency, which we have through the legislation enacted by parliament.

Sir Isaac Newton once refused to publish the results of certain experiments he had made, saying that the publication might serve to widen the circle of his acquaintance, "a thing I chiefly study to decline." Our economists do not seem, so far as mere publicity is concerned, to share Sir Isaac's aloofness; their love of society is so great as sometimes to appear promiscuous; so it must be that a kind of freemasonry among them seals their lips against revealing the prodigious truths of which they are possessed.

Yes, sir. Then I will not mention this further at present. But my point is that in regard to all the money spent by the government, each item of expenditure should be authorized by and payment made by the minister concerned. The minister of any department has an allotment of so many hundred thousands, so many millions of dollars for his department. According to my view of ministerial responsibility, responsible government and parliamentary control the minister should have the right not only to authorize an expenditure but also to control the payment of that expenditure, in order to be responsible to parliament for the disbursement made on that account. I hope I make myself clear in that regard. Some years ago under the previous administration the whole financial system of the dominion government was entirely changed; instead of having payments made under the authority of the minister concerned they are now made only by the Department of Finance under the authority of the comptroller of the treasury who is himself under the authority of the Minister of Finance. I submit that we should follow the practice which was in force in this country for a hundred years; from 1834, the time of the ninety-two resolutions-it was put in force six years later in 1840-to 1934 we had responsible government in this country, but since 1934 all payments are made by the Department of Finance and not by the ministers of the departments concerned.
[The Chairman.]
There are now no accountants in the departments who are not under the Minister of Finance. The minister concerned has no authority over the accountants in his department. Here in the House of Commons we have an accountant, a very able man; but he is not one of our officers; he is not under the authority of Mr. Speaker; he is under the authority of the comptroller of the treasury who is under the authority of the Minister of Finance. To this I strongly object on constitutional grounds, because each minister should be responsible for his own department, and if he is not responsible for the payment he cannot be held responsible for incurring any expenditure. Further, according to my view, in the present situation all the estimates should be submitted by the Minister of Finance himself, because he is responsible for the payment. I do not see how any other minister can come with them save the Minister of Finance, who through his officials authorizes every payment made. I do not see how any other minister can come and justify the administration of his department, because he administers practically nothing. I do not blame this government for that legislation, far from it; it was imposed on parliament by the previous administration, but it is all wrong. The former Prime Minister used to say that he needed to have it that way in order to get information more quickly. Last year, two months after the expiration of the fiscal year, I telephoned to a high official of the Department of Finance to know the exact amount of the debt of Canada. He told me he had not ascertained it yet. As I say, that was two months after the expiration of the fiscal year. There is no progress in that.
Another point is that with accountants in the various departments to check the expenditures and make the payments under the authority of the minister they become familiar with the work of the department. There is no man in the civil service who can be familiar with the expenditures of all departments. I defy the comptroller of the treasury or anyone in the Department of Finance ta be able to justify each expenditure in the various branches of the department; it is beyond the mental ability and the physical capacity of any man. Therefore I hope that some day the Minister of Finance will consider what is being done at Westminster. The proposal was made at Westminster to have officers of the treasury in the departments ; this was refused by the mother of parliaments. I do not intend to take up more than a few minutes, but I should like to indicate my view in regard to this resolution. One advantage of the issue of currency, as pointed out especially in the last parliament, is that it is a means whereby the credit of the country can be drawn upon without having to pay interest on the use of that credit. For that reason I understand that the present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) at that time urged the issue of $400,000,000 in currency, to be used in part towards the payment of the national debt, having in mind that if that were dohe it would avoid the payment of interest to the extent it was so used. I am 100 per cent in support of that view. I think the extent to which we can issue currency and pay the national debt and avoid payment of interest on that debt without in any way dislocating the set-up in the country is the extent to which we should go.
As was pointed out by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens), the amount of currency in circulation in Canada is about $22 per capita, compared with $42 per capita in the United States. If we issued the same amount of money per capita in Canada as they have in issue in the United States we could issue another $220,000,000 and use that money to retire interest-bearing debt. By so doing we would save no less a sum than $7,700,000 annually. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) says the reason why we have not as much money in issue in Canada as they have in the United States is that the Canadian people have confidence in our banking system, as a result of which, instead of keeping currency on hand they deposit their money in the bank and use cheques. The result is simply this, that since we have $220,000,000 less currency in issue
on account of the people of Canada having confidence in their banking system they are penalized to the extent of $7,700,000 annually. While that may be the actual reason why we have not so much currency in issue in order to do our business, it is no reason in the world why it should be so. Why should we pay interest on that sum of money just because the banks can get by with less or business can get by without that money being in issue. I do not think it can be argued that we could not put that amount of money into circulation in this country without in any way dislocating our banking set-up. As I say, if we did put that amount of money into circulation we would save $7,700,000 every year.
When I suggested last year that we put several hundred million dollars in issue on which we would not have to pay interest it was stated that under our banking system the banks made loans or investments, or tend to do so, at the rate of ten dollars for every dollar of currency put out, and that if you put $600,000,000 of currency in issue, under our present system this would inevitably result in the long run in the banks putting out by way of loans and investments something around $6,000,000,000. At that time I suggested that if the banks showed any such tendency unduly to inflate their loans and investments you could take control and prevent them from doing so. The United States increased the amount of currency in circulation, and in order to prevent the banks from unduly inflating credit they increased their reserve requirement, as I understand it, from ten to twenty cents for every dollar invested or loaned by the bank. In other words the reserve requirement in the United States to-day is twenty cents for every dollar loaned or invested, whereas in Canada the legal requirement is still only five cents per dollar loaned or invested. No one can tell me that we cannot thus control our banks by taking control at any time over the reserve required. We can put twice the amount of money in circulation and double the reserve requirement if necessary in order to prevent the banks from inflating their credits or investments by a single cent. As a matter of fact, we have in the past three years to a very limited extent actually increased our currency in circulation, but the banks claim they cannot, under present conditions, greatly increase loans to commercial institutions. The result is that they have not actually increased their loans or invests ments in that direction and so the inflation of credit predicted has not yet occurred. So I submit that, under present conditions, without changing our reserve requirement we could

increase the amount of currency in circulation without fear of immediate credit inflation. But as we did so, to make entirely certain that the banks would not take advantage of the situation, I say we should take power to increase the reserve requirement in order to prevent that inflation of credit if it threatened.
The situation in regard to this resolution, therefore, is simply this. There is roughly $400,000,000 of this debt Canada owes and which it is proposed to refund by reborrowing at interest which is payable within Canada. I submit that we could require the Bank of Canada to print $400,000,000 of notes and pay that $400,000,000 as it came due with those Bank of Canada notes. As I understand it, the average rate of interest to-day is roughly three and a half per cent, and by adopting that course we could save $14,000,000 of interest every year. I think that is worth considering. If it be said that the moment you put $400,000,000 of new currency into circulation the banks are going to loan or make investments to the extent of $4,000,000,000, I say you can prevent that by increasing your reserve requirement, or by taking power to do so. You would not need to increase it; the very threat would prevent the banks from going to any extreme.
I welcome very much the suggestion of the Minister of Finance that the servants of the people, the officials of the Bank of Canada, should be called before the representatives of the people of Canada to explain what use they are making of the control we have given them over the currency and credit of this country. I welcome that because it seems to me that they should be asked, among other things, if it would not be feasible for us to take the step I have just suggested. I hope the minister will announce at a very early date that this procedure will be followed, because it seems to me high time we put looking after our old and sick people, looking after our unemployment situation and giving opportunity to our young people, above the payment of unnecessary interest on government debt. To me that is the one place where to-day parliament can save money. We hear speeches these days from Toronto, for example, suggesting that if certain business supermen were in control of the dominion government they could save money; but if you asked them where they would save it to any great extent they would not be able to say. Would they eliminate help to the farmers of western Canada? Would they eliminate help to the fishermen of the east? Would they eliminate help to the unemployed or old folks of Ontario or Quebec or elsewhere? Where would they save the money? This is one place, Mr. 
Chairman, where it would be possible to save money in order to do the things that we as a people want to do. So I welcome the opportunity to have the officials of the Bank of Canada, whom I regard as experts in their particular line, come before the representatives of the people in the banking and commerce committee and explain why it is not possible-if they so think-for us to increase our currency in that way, at the same time preventing undue inflation.
I think the ultimate ideal should be this, that you should gradually increase the amount of currency in circulation and gradually increase your reserve requirement until you have every cent owing by the banks by way of deposit in the banks-amounting, as hon. members know, to almost $3,000,000,000-covered by money issued by the government of this country. Thereby you would save over $100,000,000 in interest and you would prevent the present inflation of credit by the banks. Under our present system the banks are, in effect, little, private mints- On the basis of their reserve requirement they can extend credit at the rate of ten dollars to one dollar to the country, which means purchasing power created as the money loaned is subject to check by the government or other borrower and is received by those to whom the cheques are paid as if they were money. When there is a threat of bad conditions the banks begin to draw in their loans and destroy purchasing power. As a matter of fact, one of the common sayings of the period since 1933-34 has been, "Where has the money gone? There is just as much money in the country'as ever." As a matter of fact, there was not as much money in the country, because the banks had drawn in loans represented by deposits in the banks against which cheques could be issued. They had,-as I remember the figures,-contracted those loans to private enterprise to the extent of roughly $900,000,000 between 1929 and 1934. The marvel to me is this, that with that contraction going on in the money to do the business of the country, over the short period of only five years, it did not absolutely wreck our economic structure.
I am glad the Minister of Finance once more is well enough to carry on in the vigorous manner he has demonstrated this afternoon. I have every respect for him. But when he worries about increasing, say, the amount of currency in circulation per capita in Canada to a point at least equal to the amount in circulation in the United States, sufficient to save that interest I have mentioned ; when I think about the financial

I submit that the one way of getting away from the banking system engaging in periods of undue inflation and then engaging in periods of undue deflation is gradually to increase the reserve requirements to a point where the banks will be able truly to say that for every dollar they owe depositors they have a dollar on hand. To-day, as I pointed out, by law they can loan out $20 for every dollar they have in legal reserve.
As I pointed out, that leads to a condition where, when the country wants to borrow, it must pay interest. It leads to these inflational booms. It leads to the destruction of purchasing power in deflationary periods. It leads, whether we like it or not, to the very thing that is happening to-day. The people do not know the reason why our system is not functioning, and they are inclined to blame our parliamentary and democratic institutions. We must make that system . function, or it will ultimately be destroyed. Those people who seek power by blaming the present government, but without offering any policy of their own and who, if the people believed them, would find themselves in power without any policy, and would carry on for five years without solving the fundamental problems of the country, are playing with the very future of our democratic system.
I would say that no man should seek power in Canada if all he has to offer is a palliative, something which would not go to the root of matters in solving the problems of this dominion. If any man does that, he is playing with the confidence of the democracy of Canada.
I submit the one place where the system does not work to-day is right in the realm of currency and credit. That is the one burden- the payment of interest on the use of its own credit-which the government must shed. It is one place where the credit power of Canada can be placed at the service of the people of Canada, to the extent that the Canadian people should be permitted to use their entire man power, and their entire brain power, to develop the resources God put within their control. They should be permitted to work at full capacity to produce wealth.
And if the system is not working to put our unemployed to work and to develop what, after all, is theirs-the resources of Canada- then that system is not working properly.
Unemployment is not a scourge. Those who are unemployed to-day should be regarded as an asset, not a liability. They should be regarded as people who could be put to work to produce real wealth. Then, after we have our entire machinery working to produce the maximum amount of wealth, there would be no difficulty in seeing to it that the people of Canada enjoyed or consumed that wealth. Sherbrooke, Que., Jan. 24.-Canada's debt burden gradually is lowering the general standard of living, G. W. Spinney of Montreal, general manager of the Bank of Montreal, said in an address prepared for delivery to the associated boards of trade of Quebec eastern townships to-night. The indifferent attitude towards mounting government debts threatens the country's welfare, he said.
Mr. Spinney stressed the seriousness of the drain relief expenditures and railway deficits made upon the country's resources without showing tangible returns and he urged that effective action be taken towards practising government economy and solving the unemployment and railway problems. "A great deal is heard nowadays of the effectiveness of the totalitarian states and it does seem to be a fact that unless general government administration is improved, the very foundations of our democratic forms of government may be threatened," he said.
"The primary threat to the welfare of this country lies in our indifferent attitude towards mounting debts. Federal and provincial government indebtedness is ever on the increase and some municipal bodies are shaping their courses in the same direction. maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1939

speechtext:
Hon. P. J. A. CARDIN (Minister of Public Works) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize the Minister of Public Works on behalf of his majesty to enter into an agreement to pay to the corporation of the city of Ottawa the sum of $100,000 for the year ending July 1, 1939.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1939
speechtext:
I do not wish to oppose this vote; I think it is a very good one; but there are one or two points about this agreement which I think should be explained to

City of Ottawa Agreement
the committee. It would be a good thing if the federal district commission were to take the members of the house around a bit and show them what work is being done. I do not say there is duplication, but I refer to one or two points of this agreement.
The agreement started in 1920 at $50,000, then went to $75,000 and now it is $100,000. First there is the question of snow cleaning. At the present time the city of Ottawa is doing very good work in that connection. Snow cleaning is done partly by the city, and then there are in the city a number of parks and driveways and federal property on which the roads are cleaned and kept in repair by the federal district commission. The basis of the $100,000 payment is consideration for services rendered by the city of Ottawa to the government: water supply, police, fire protection and other civic services. There is a principle underlying this. The principle follows what was done in the capital cities in New Zealand and Australia; they receive something in exchange for the civic services given. For example, in New South Wales the government maintains the police force; in other places, the fire department. There are other cities in Canada where there are these federal buildings-Montreal, Toronto, Hamilton, Winnipeg, Vancouver. They give the federal authority the very same civic services which Ottawa is giving, and good services; yet this principle is not applied to these places. It should apply. The Ontario government are giving to the municipalities part of the liquor licence revenues. The municipalities are now demanding something from the fees collected for motor vehicle licences. Some years ago the dominion government took from the municipalities the income tax. From confederation down to 1918 the income tax was the exclusive field of the municipalities. In 1918 the government no doubt needed the money on account of the war expenditures and they imposed a duplicate tax. In some provinces there is a triplicate tax on incomes. The Ontario government has taken the municipal income tax away altogether and established a flat rate for the province, which, some say, works a hardship to the larger municipalities especially. I am not objecting to this Ottawa vote; I am glad to see Ottawa get it, but the same principle should be applied to other places, when one considers how the municipalities have had their field of taxation invaded by federal and provincial power.
This $100,000 is not all. Parks, playgrounds, squares and driveways within the confines of the municipality of Ottawa are maintained at the expense of the dominion. From the
annual report of the federal district commission for the year ending March 31, 1936, it will be seen that there was a contribution of $217,000 from the dominion. Then the report goes on to refer to these public improvements within the city of Ottawa. The city I come from is paying for roads for fifteen miles around the city through the Toronto highways commission, and also for No. 7 highway to Brampton it is paying about $200,000 on capital and maintenance. Then, in the city of Ottawa the federal district commission pays for certain municipal services on these parks, driveways and squares. In Toronto we have a harbour commission, and we might just as well ask the dominion to pay for University avenue, Fleet street, the exhibition park, waterfront and other places in the riding of the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Spence). The report of the federal district commission refers to 137,100 perennials and annual flowering plants sent out from the commission's greenhouse at Rockcliffe to be planted in the commission's parks and government grounds throughout the city, as well as a number of trees and shrubs. Then there is $58,385 for construction and development, including new greenhouses, Elgin street subway improvements, and so on. The total disbursements amounted to $244,389. That also covers the amount spent on Rideau Hall and the grounds, improvements, maintenance and so on.

speechtext: I would ask all hon. members to keep order. It is very difficult for the Hansard reporter to hear the remarks of the hon. member who has the floor.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1939
speechtext:
Last year we provided another Ottawa district vote of $100,000 for the acquisition of land and for surveys in connection with a national parkway in the Gatineau valley district and the Laurentian hills, and I should like my hon. friends to listen to this. It is said we do no work here, but some of our friends in another place in this building have gone on a sit-down strike, and on three weeks more holidays, expecting us to do all the work. That is not what they do in the senate in Washington, the Ottawa of the south. There they stay on the job, and it is not hard for them in their senate to find work. Speaking of the unemployed, I think the other chamber should take up this problem. Why do they not do something about it as they did in the senate in Washington in 1927?
To return to the question of $100,000 for the new Gatineau and district park, the learned and respected clerk of the house gave
City oj Ottawa Agreement

an address a few years ago in regard to what could be done to improve this city and district and make it fit to be the capital of this great country. I think from what I saw of that address the clerk would have made a good parks engineer. I do not see the hon. member for Wright (Mr. Leduc) in the chamber, and I hope he will not think I am objecting to this second item. He has a splendid historic county and district, and I do not object to the creation of a national park there; far from it. But I believe that with the present unemployment situation, when we cannot provide the necessities of life for our own people, we should exercise a little care in the expenditure of our money. I believe we are tearing down too many buildings in Ottawa, and ruining the continuity of business on some of the business streets. That is particularly so here in Ottawa. The assessment here has been reduced and the city is losing a large amount of money every year. All this money has to be provided in some way. In the ordinary city expenditures in connection with parks, their expenditures are charged to capital, but I understand that under this government agreement these moneys must come out of income.
It was said by the two Ottawa newspapers that I was unfair to this city. That is not so. I should like to see Ottawa get everything it is entitled to, because I think they have a good city government here. But I do say the government is taking away the revenues of the large municipalities; in addition those municipalities are charged with the cost of relief, and I submit that other places should get equality of treatment. The Minister of Labour brought down a program to provide works for the relief of unemployment in the municipalities, and he also announced that the new division of the cost of direct relief would be forty per cent by the dominion, forty per cent by the province and twenty per cent by the municipality. What does the province of Ontario do? It takes the forty per cent which it is supposed to give the municipalities, chisels it down to about twenty per cent for January, February and March of this year, and does not give them the forty per cent expected for three months.
We should follow the practice that is followed in Australia, where the federal government grants a subsidy, bonus and subvention to the municipalities in compensation for the tax-exempt federal properties and the municipal services rendered, or gives them a share of the income tax collected. In some of the states to the south the state capital is given

a subsidy in compensation for certain municipal services, but in Canada this government gives nothing, except to the city of Ottawa. In the city of Hamilton, for example, the municipality has to supply police protection, fire protection, local improvements and so on, and the city gets nothing in return for aid to the federal government. I think the time has come when we should have equality of treatment by the federal power in regard to these municipal services. I do not oppose this vote; I am not opposed to the creation of the Gatineau park, but I do think it is time something was done for the other municipalities. Real estate is being burdened as a result of these federal and provincial taxes so that to-day the holding of real estate is a liability. Mortgages are being foreclosed and industrial workers are being put on the street as a result of the heavy taxes on real estate for relief. As you no doubt are aware, Mr. Chairman, the taxes on an average property constitute a rent in themselves, and the taxes on the homes of workingmen are about twice that. It really amounts, in many instances, to confiscation of property. No wonder the home building program has not been a success, when one considers the way in which these taxes are put on real estate. A man may own a property with a first mortgage, a second mortgage, a chattel mortgage on some of his goods, a bill of sale on the remainder, a lien note, a building lien on the property and every other kind of lien. So he cannot qualify for a loan either from a bank or from a shark loan company.
I hope the minister will take some action in the near future to remedy this situation. In Toronto we have a federal building on Front street covering nearly a block, on which no municipal taxes are paid. The city has to supply that building with fire and police protection; it has to furnish water at cut-rates; it has to construct a road and sidewalk in front of the property, and all that sort of thing. When Sir James Whitney became premier of Ontario, he introduced a policy under which the provincial government paid for local improvements such as sidewalks in front of provincial public buildings, parks and so on. If that is not done, the cost of these works has to come out of the general tax rate, and it becomes a burden on real estate. So I believe we have come to a time when the government must do something in order to help real estate and give other cities something. Otherwise we shall be carrying on a policy of favouritism, robbing collective Paul to pay selective Peter.

City of Ottawa Agreement
What is the principle of this legislation? These are moneys to which other municipalities in Canada are entitled too. What kind of legislation is that? Would the hon. member for Parkdale adopt such a principle in connection with his York highways commission? I hope some hon. members will have the opportunity of travelling on some of his highways, because he has a fine type of highway there.
I say the time has come for a change in jprinciple whereby some of these moneys might go to the other cities and towns in which the other 243 members live, so that they may get the same treatment as the city of Ottawa.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1939
speechtext: Is the vote of $100,000 supposed to compensate Ottawa for the property which has been removed from the assessment rolls, and therefore no longer revenue producing so far as taxation is concerned? I might point out to the minister that it is the opinion of several people in this city, particularly business men, that the removal of property from the assessment rolls, property which has been taken over by the federal government, has imposed a heavy burden upon the other taxpayers of the city. It is suggested to me that if the federal properties were called upon to pay taxes, instead of the sum of $100,000 the cost would be close to $1,000,000. I should like to have the minister's opinion as to the object of the payment of $100,000?

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1939
speechtext:
May I say to the hon. member who has just taken his seat that the question he raised was discussed in 1920 when this agreement became effective. At that time the city of Ottawa made a heavy claim on the federal government for compensation for the very things the hon. member has just mentioned. They claimed that because the federal government was taking over or expropriating certain properties the city was being deprived of taxes which otherwise it would derive from those properties. Upon that occasion they made a claim, although at this time I do not remember exactly what the amount was. As a result, however, of discussions between representatives of the city and the government an agreement was reached whereby all those claims would be wiped out, and the city of Ottawa would undertake to protect federal buildings from fire and, in addition, supply the water used on the parks for sprinkling purposes.
The sum of $100,000 has been paid to Ottawa since 1925 or 1926. Prior to that time, under the terms of the agreement of 1920, the annual grant was $75,000. Those payments have been made for the services I mentioned, namely fire protection and sprinkling service, and, if not directly, at least indirectly to help to compensate for loss of revenue in taxes. Such a compensation was claimed by the city when discussion of an agreement took place in 1920. The agreement has been renewed every year, and the resolution now before us provides for the introduction of a bill to renew the agreement for another year.
The federal government has been paying the city of Ottawa certain sums of money for a very long time. The first payment was made in 1899 for the reasons pointed out by the hon. member. Since that time the federal government has continued to contribute money to the city. I believe I am free to say that the agreement is not wholly satisfactory to the city. I am informed the city council had in mind asking the federal government for an increase to at least $150,000. The federal authorities, however, thought the present amount was a proper one and could see no reason for increasing it, particularly in view of the fact that we are making other expenditures in Ottawa which in certain ways help to relieve the situation so far as unemployment is concerned. We have thought that for this year at least it would be fair to renew the agreement as it is and pay the same amount as we paid last year.
The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) mentions the fact that other cities might claim the same privileges. That has been considered. But if we began to apply the same principle and attempted to compensate all cities in Canada where there are public buildings, I am afraid very serious complications and difficulties would arise in adjusting the claims of the different cities.
There is justification for the present vote for the city of Ottawa, because it is the capital of the country. We are supposed to be a little more generous towards the capital city than towards other cities. In addition to that, the federal government has much more property in Ottawa than at any other point in Canada, which may serve as an additional justification for the payment to this city. I know there are public buildings in Montreal and Toronto, but the value of those properties does not compare with the value of federal government properties in Ottawa. Although I should like to see something done in other Canadian cities, I am inclined to be a little more generous towards Ottawa, a capital city of which we are proud, and for which we ought to do the best we can, according to our financial ability to provide developments and betterments.
City of Ottawa Agreement

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1939
speechtext:
I have no objection at all to, in fact I support, the vote for $100,000 which the government intends to pay to Ottawa in lieu of taxes and other revenues of which the city is deprived by reason of the federal buildings. But I think, taking it all in all, our federal government treats Ottawa in a fairly generous way. I have not the slightest objection to the improvements which, as a matter of policy, the government are bringing about in the city. In fact, I approve most of them. But at the same time the people of Ottawa are not appreciative of that very fact. They seem to accept these things as a matter of course. There is really no compulsion upon the government to go to all the expense they have incurred over a period of years to beautify the city and to make it a worthy capital of the Dominion of Canada.
There is no city in the dominion which receives anything like the amount of support from either a provincial or federal government that is received by the city of Ottawa. And, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), the federal government provides parks and driveways in the city which in all other cities of the dominion are entirely a municipal responsibility. Going back over the years I can find nothing worth while calling an improvement that has been initiated and carried out by the people of this city. I have made inquiries on the point and have tried to learn about anything by way of beautification of the city which has been done by the city, but so far I have been unable to find anything whatsoever.
I do not know the exact amount that is being spent by the federal government upon what might be called purely civic enterprises, such as parks, playgrounds and other schemes of beautification, but I believe the amount would run into many millions of dollars. The amounts mentioned a moment ago by the hon. member for Broadview when he was speaking of the money spent by the government in Ottawa did not cover everything. I am wondering whether the Minister of Public Works has in his possession information as to the full amount spent in Ottawa each year by the federal government. I am not asking for the salaries paid to people employed by the government, but I should like to know what it costs the government, so far as Ottawa is concerned, to maintain these parks and driveways, to pay for the removal of snow from the streets and to keep up other improvements which in other cities are looked upon as entirely civic matters. I wonder if the Minister of Public Works has that information with him at the moment.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1939
speechtext: I regret I am not in a position to give that information to my hon. friend, for a very good reason. The works which he has just mentioned are carried on by the federal district commission, which is not under the Department of Public Works. That commission speaks in this house through the Minister of Finance. I believe my hon. friend could get the information he is asking for from the report of the federal district commission. If my hon. friend is interested in having that information, I can have the figures prepared for him.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1939
speechtext: I have pleasure in supporting this resolution. I supported resolutions in former years when the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart) was Minister of Public Works. I think all members, no matter from where they come, should support this vote. After all, any impression that a foreigner may gain of our country is helped by the impression he gets of our capital city. I believe this money has been efficiently administered by this and former governments. This is a resolution that should not require much discussion, and I am glad to give it my support.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1939
speechtext: I should like to associate myself with the last speaker, the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Hanson). I feel that Ottawa should be a beautiful city. A thing of beauty is a joy forever, its loveliness increases and it will never pass into nothingness. If there is anything that can be done by way of relief for the people, I think it should be something that will add beauty to our cities. We should be willing to do all we can to help to make Ottawa a beautiful city. I believe this $100,000 can be put to doing good work at this time, especially with the great plan they have in mind for the beautification of the city. This is an annual grant. I am certain that Ottawa has become much more beautiful since we came down here. Beauty is truth, and truth is beauty. That is all we know in this world, and all we need to know.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1939
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there is no doubt that the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Hanson) is willing to support a proposition of this kind. He got a very nice building in his little town. I do not begrudge him it; I only hope that Prince Rupert grows to a size where that building will be in proportion to the size of the town. Every on: seems to be willing to support this vote of $100,000, so I am not going to oppose it. However, as the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) said a minute ago, certain other cities in Canada should also receive some consideration. The hon. member referred to the many services rendered by Toronto. There are in that city

City of Ottawa Agreement
a great number of public buildings from which the city receives no taxes. I think the Minister of Public Works should include something in the estimates for Toronto to cover the work that city is doing.
I understand the city has been communicating with the Minister of Labour in an effort 4o obtain a grant to help in the construction of a sewage disposal plant. We have a plant now, but it is inadequate. It is almost dangerous because some of the sewage is running into the lake without being treated properly. A proposition of that kind would employ thousands of people for the next two or three years, and better results would be obtained than if the money was spent in many other ways. It will cost about $15,000,000, and I understand the provincial government has offered to pay twenty-five per cent. The city was hoping that this government would pay twenty-five per cent, which would leave about eight million dollars for the city to spend itself.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1939
speechtext: Does that come under beautification?

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1939
speechtext:
No, it is better than beautification; it has to do with the health of the people. We do not want our lake polluted with sewage from any city. This matter should receive attention. I hope the Minister of Labour, with all the money he has under his control, or the Minister of Public Works, will see that this is done. It would be something of lasting credit to this government and to this country. The taxpayer of Toronto has been literally overwhelmed paying taxes. Relief there is getting worse and worse every year. No matter what anyone may say, relief in Toronto is getting no better.
The hon. member for Broadview referred to the Toronto and York roads commission. At one time I was chairman of this commission, and I have been a member for the last twenty-four years. When my hon. friend was mayor of the city, an arrangement was made between the county of York and the city of Toronto whereby the city paid twenty-five per cent of the cost of maintaining roads extending all over the county. The provincial government was to pay fifty per cent of the cost. This arrangement covers roads extending out as far as fifty and sixty miles to the borders of Ontario, Peel and other counties. No doubt York is a rich county and has done great things in its time. There are over 400 miles of roads in York. The present chairman of the roads commission is my old-time friend, Senator O'Connor. I am sorry to say that he has been ill in Florida, but perhaps hon. members will be glad to know that a letter 71492-65
was received last Monday by the commission stating that he was getting better and expected to be back by the middle of April or the first of May.
I am tired of hearing people call Toronto a hog town. " Hog-town " pays a great deal of money to this government by way of taxation. Just consider the business done in the post office and the money taken in at the customs.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1939
speechtext: More income tax is paid there than in any other city in Canada.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1939
speechtext: We cannot take all the credit for that because Toronto is the centre of the district. But I do get sick and tired of people referring to Toronto as "hog-town." I have lived in Toronto for forty-eight years and I have been behind every big municipal proposition and development carried on in that city. I have supported the program of bridge construction, road building, the improvement of the harbour front and many other useful developments. I am proud of Toronto at all times. Not only has it contributed largely to the building of roads in the county of York, but it contributed $200,000 to Ontario towards expenditures in other counties of the province. Hon. J. E. MICHAUD (Minister of Fisheries) moved the second reading of Bill No. 15, to amend the Fisheries Act, 1932.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext: Clause 1-Repeal.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext:
Before clause 1 is dealt with I should like to introduce an amendment to a section which comes prior to this one, which is section 57. The section I want to amend is No. 32. I therefore move:
That section 32 of the Fisheries Act, 1932, chapter 42, is hereby amended by inserting the following as subsection 2 thereof:
2. No one shall use a salmon trap net in any of the Pacific waters of Canada.
I do that in order to get an opportunity to press the need of this reform in the interests of the fishing industry and of the fishermen of British Columbia, and also to give the minister an opportunity to state his policy on the matter.
It will be recalled that on January 23 of this year I asked him a couple of questions on the orders of the day. I asked him if his
71492-65J
attention had been called to a paragraph in the Vancouver Sun to the effect that the senate of the state of Washington was preparing and would shortly introduce two fish trap bills that would enable fish traps to be restored in the state of Washington waters. The second question I asked was: In view of that fact, was he, that is the minister, prepared to take the responsibility of maintaining our traps, only four in number, as against their 219, knowing that the results will be that our catch in those waters will drop from 80 per cent, as it is at present, to 30 per cent, as it used to be when the United States traps were operating? The minister replied that the question of the advisability of reciprocating or of maintaining the policy of issuing fish trap licences was being considered at the present time-that is at that date, January 23, which is three and a half weeks ago. We have heard nothing more yet, and the matter will have to be decided, I should think, within the next few days in any case, because the season is coming on.
The fishermen out there have quite recently organized very strongly in this matter. They are proposing to put on a campaign of a very considerable extent and of their own accord. Last year I presented to the house a petition signed by almost 10,000 people from British Columbia against the fish traps being used any further; and now the unions of fishermen have taken the matter up. One union alone comprising 1,400 practical working fishermen are proposing, as I have said, to get up a campaign. They have support from boards of trade, the trades and labour council, and the city council. They have been stirred up by the notice I have referred to that there was the proposal to re-install traps on the Washington side, and particularly on account of the fact that the argument the trap owners on the United States side were using, are going to use, and do use, is that Canada has not kept faith and has not taken out her traps. I quote a few lines from one of the organizations:
The organized fishermen of British Columbia are at present conducting a vigorous campaign against the continued operation of the fish traps at Sooke, especially on account of the fact that Washington interests are attempting to reintroduce traps in sites over the border.
This is from another union, which says:
Our fight against the issue of fish trap licences is started again. We are holding a series of meetings and starting three petitions, one to be signed by fishermen, one by sports fishermen, and one by business men.
Then I have a record of a conference, as they call it, which was held in Vancouver on
Fisheries Act Amendment

January 23, 24 and 25, attended by delegates from the following bodies:	Prince Rupert
Fishermen's Cooperative Association, North Island Trollers Cooperative Association, Fishermen's Cooperative Association, Inc., Kyu-quot Trollers Cooperative Association, representing over 1,400 individual fishing boat owners, and the resolution they passed was as follows, of which a copy was sent to the minister at that time:
Whereas the department of fisheries of the Dominion of Canada has promised the fishermen of British Columbia to eliminate all fish traps this coming year;-
I do not think it was this year; they promised it three years ago.
-And whereas the state of Washington is now considering the reinstatement of such traps in order to obtain its share of the fish now being caught by the traps in the British Columbia coast waters;
And whereas the depletion of the salmon run calls for strong conservation measures in order to preserve these resources;
And whereas the fishing boats engaged in the trolling, purse seining and gill netting industry are in a position to create a livelihood for a greater number of men than are at present employed by the trap owners, and at the same time provide for the better escapement of the salmon to the spawning grounds.
Therefore be it resolved that we, the members of these associations-
And I will not read them again.
-in convention assembled this twenty-third day of January, 1939, do strongly recommend to the fisheries department that all fish traps shall be completely removed from the waters of British Columbia.
I might continue and go thoroughly into the history of the matter to enlighten those hon. members to whom it is not familiar; but it might save time if I stopped here and gave the minister an opportunity to express his policy on the matter, because I am hopeful, from the representations which have been made to him and from his attitude in the house the other day, when he intimated that it was being considered, that he may now be in a position to state that he has decided to stop these traps being issued any further in these waters.
