speechtext:
The first part of clause 2 is, as the minister stated when he introduced the bill, for the purpose of making more definite his power to collect certain sums for the maintenance of fish ladders or a substitute for those fish ladders. As far as that part of it goes, I quite agree with it. But I am doubtful about the clause which he did not mention. that is subsection 2 which reads:
Such lump sum or annual sum shall be payable at such time or times as the minister may direct-
That is all right.
-and may be sued for and recovered with full costs of suit in the exchequer court of Canada.
The previous way was that if any man did not fulfil the obligation imposed on him by the minister under section 57, then by the last clause of paragraph (d) of section 57 he was liable to a penalty of not less than $4 and not more than $20 for each day or part thereof during which such notice was not complied with. Now the minister changes that into a provision by which he can sue this man in the exchequer court and recover the amount with full costs of suit. That might result in a condition which would vitiate the very object the minister has in view. An exchequer court proceeding is a long business. If I remember rightly, the exchequer court sits only once a year on the Pacific coast. The section that was in the bill before which provided for a penalty of so much a day was easily enforced by either
Fisheries Act Amendment

summary conviction or indictment; the minister could get quick action. Assume this condition: A logger has an area of timber to log; it suits him to put a dam across the mouth of the outlet from a lake, and he stops the passage of the fish. Representations are made to the department here, and they write the logger but he does not pay any attention. Time goes on, and he is cutting his timber. Presently the minister is compelled to tell him that if he does not put in a proper ladder he will be sued in the exchequer court. The man just laughs at the minister and his officials and goes on logging. Finally the case is brought up in the exchequer court, but by the time that court sits out there and judgment is rendered the man has finished logging that area and has moved on, leaving the river ruined with nothing whatever to show for it. While I quite agree with the first part of the provision, which makes it easy and convenient for the minister to collect any sum he thinks proper, I think it would be better to retain the penalty to which this man may be liable if he puts in a dam in defiance of the government order. This penalty of $20 a day could be enforced readily and speedily by a justice of the peace or some similar court. I suggest that to the minister, who is himself a lawyer.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext:
I think the hon. member altogether misunderstood what I said when the bill was introduced. The object of this amendment is to enable the government, through the department, to collect the amount which may be assessed against any person or company interfering with the ascent of fish in certain cases; but it does not apply in all cases. If the hon. member will look at section 57 of the act, he will find in paragraphs (a), (b), (c) and (d) four provisions which enable the department to see that there are proper openings in canals or rivers for the ascent of fish. I think under paragraphs (a), (c) and (d) a case such as that mentioned by the hon. member could be dealt with. An obstruction at the mouth of a river, for example, a dam, by logs or anything else, could be opened up and the person owning the obstruction or placing it there could be fined. But the purpose of the amendment to paragraph (b) of the act is to provide for cases much more important than cases such as my hon. friend mentions. Let me read the first part of this section: Every owner or occupier of a slide, dam or other obstruction across or in any stream,-
(a) Where the minister determines it to be necessary in the public interest that a canal around a dam or a fish-pass therein, should (Mr. Neill.]
exist, who, after three days' notice in writing, neglects or refuses to provide a durable and efficient fishway or canal, or who neglects or refuses to maintain the same in a good and effective condition in such place and of such form and capacity as will admit of the passage of fish;-
shall be liable to a penalty of not less than four dollars and not more than twenty dollars for each day or part of a day during which such notice is not complied with.
This is not affected at all by the amendment, and paragraph (b) now reads:
(b) Where the minister determines that the provision of an effective fishway or canal around the slide, dam or other obstruction is not feasible, or that the spawning areas above such slide, dam or other obstruction are destroyed, who after thirty days' notice in writing, neglects or refuses to pay the minister such sum or sums of money as he may require to construct, operate and maintain such complete hatchery establishment as will in the opinion of the minister meet the requirements for maintaining the annual return of migratory fish; shall be liable to a penalty of not less than four dollars and not more than twenty dollars for each day or part of a day during which such notice is not complied with.
My hon. friend will readily see the difficulty of enforcing the provisions of paragraph (b), with the sanction provided at the end of that clause. There is no way of collecting the amount determined by the minister as necessary to provide for the continued propagation of fish in those waters. So, in order that the provisions of this act may be effectively enforced, we are providing for a court in which to sue and collect the amount which has been assessed. It may be said that the exchequer court is a tribunal difficult of access, but it will be seen that the amounts which may be determined under paragraph (b) may be no trifling sum. Where it is not feasible 'to build a fishway it may be necessary to build a hatchery, and the cost of maintaining a hatchery to replace the natural propagation that would result from the natural ascent of fish over an obstruction might be a large amount. I have in mind one case where it would be not less than $4,00(7 or $5,000 a year. This is to provide for cases where, for instance, substantial power dams which may be built in some waters would absolutely destroy the possibility of the natural propagation of fish.
So I believe the ordinary cases can still be dealt with, and those violating the act can be penalized, under the remaining paragraphs of this section; but we had to provide an extraordinary remedy in order that we might be enabled to collect the amount of money that might be assessed in other cases, in addition to the fine.

Fisheries Act Amendment

When the 1938 crop was coming on the market, world conditions were different from those of either 1936 or 1937. It became evident that the unsettled situation in Europe, together with the enormous world production, would result in a low world price.
It was also evident that if war resulted in Europe in the fall of 1938, as it threatened to do, wheat would rise rapidly in price. It was therefore considered that an emergency existed which, together with the difficulties experienced by the wheat producers in the years immediately preceding, necessitated the establishment of a minimum price which would in all probability pay a bonus to the wheat producing farmer.
The price was set at 80 cents a bushel, which has resulted to date in paying to the producer what amounts to a bonus of from fifteen to twenty cents a bushel. I think a bonus of even that amount can be justified for this year under all the circumstances. It can be justified as the legislation has been justified from the beginning, namely, that it is dealing with an emergency condition. With the world price below the set price the board naturally gets all the wheat.
I should like to place before the committee information as to who has received the greater part of the bonus which has been paid, in order that we might have information upon which policy might be based for the handling of wheat in the future if we are going to give assistance of any kind to wheat growers.
During the last few months I have had prepared a statement of just what happened in relation to the bonus paid to date in one province, Saskatchewan, which is the largest wheat producing province in the dominion, and of course the figures I have before me are of necessity still based upon estimates, but I think the committee will realize that they are so close to what will actually happen that they can be taken as authentic.
It is estimated that Saskatchewan farmers will receive, at the rate of twenty cents a bushel on the wheat they will market, a minimum of $18,000,000 above the market value of the marketable surplus of wheat in the province in the year 1938-39 through the operation of the minimum price policy of the federal wheat board.
Let me repeat that. An average of twenty cents a bushel paid on all the marketable

wheat in Saskatchewan will net to the farmers by way of bonus 818,000,000. But if one were to estimate the net returns to the farmers of the three western provinces on the same basis of twenty cents a bushel, I am given to understand from a discussion which took place in the Alberta legislature the other day that Alberta would collect $22,800,000, although the crop acreage in that province is very much lower than the crop acreage in Saskatchewan.
Taking all three provinces, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, the estimated amount would probably reach some $48,000,000, if put on the same basis as I have estimated for Saskatchewan.
What I wish to point out in that connection is this, that all of the area in western Canada which had a complete crop failure during this past year is in Saskatchewan. There are eighty municipalities in Saskatchewan that have an average crop of less than six bushels to the acre; more than half of these have an average crop of less than four bushels to the acre; the greater part of that half have an average crop of less than three bushels to the acre, and a number of them have no bushelage whatsoever. Yet, out of $48,000,000 which will be paid out of the treasury of Canada this year, if this estimate is correct, only $18,000,000 will go to Saskatchewan, the province with the greatest acreage and with the greatest amount of difficulty because of lack of crop.
To illustrate the results from another point of view, five municipalities in Saskatchewan which have no crop at all have 1,700 farm operators, with a total wheat acreage estimated at 153,000 acres; that is, 1,700 farmers with no crop at all will receive under the bonus system nothing at all from the treasury of Canada by way of bonus on wheat, and they become a complete charge upon the treasury, first of the province, and then, because of the difficulties existing in the province in so many municipalities, indirectly a complete charge upon the treasury of the Dominion of Canada in relation to the amounts that have been paid out under the bonus itself.
If we look at the matter in another way, there are 159 municipalities in Saskatchewan, or more than half the municipalities in the province, accounting for approximately half the acreage in the province from which there is a marketable surplus, where the crop ranges from half a bushel to six bushels to the acre, with an average of 3-8 bushels to the acre for the total 159 municipalities. The total amount of price bonus received under the present system in the 159 municipalities having within them half the crop acreage will

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing
be 86,000.000, or one-third of the amount paid in to the province. In these municipalities the price bonus will have to be supplemented by relief from the government of Canada; and that assistance, as I stated the other night, for all of those within the 159 municipalities and for those in the other areas I have spoken of, has been estimated at about $9,000,000. Therefore, in addition to paying $18,000,000 by way of bonus to farmers in Saskatchewan, we shall have to pay another $9,000,000 in order to provide relief and assistance so that those who get nothing out of the bonus can live through the winter.
If we look at it in still another way, in eighty-one municipalities with wheat acreage approximating one-fifth of the total in the province and with yields per acre of marketable surplus of wheat in excess of eight bushels and ranging up to twenty-five bushels, it is estimated that the price bonus will amount to $6,000,000.
That is, you have one group of municipalities, numbering 159, with an average marketable crop of 3-8 bushels, and all farmers in that great area obtain under this system only 86,000,000. Then you have another eighty-one municipalities with an average marketable crop in bushels per acre running from nine bushels up to twenty-five, getting $6,000,000. I suggest that in this latter group is a considerable number of farmers who did not require any assistance from the government in order to make their crop a paying one this last year. Then you have another considerable number of farmers in the other vast area, who, no matter what price would have been given to them, would not have had a paying crop because the average per acre of marketable grain was only about 3-8 bushels.
Then, in seven municipalities with an average of half a bushel per acre of marketable surplus, and with 284,000 acres under wheat, the wheat board price bonus under this policy is estimated at $28,000. In seven other municipalities with a marketable surplus of wheat ranging from sixteen to twenty-two bushels to the acre, and with a wheat acreage of 192,000 acres, which is almost 90,000 acres less than were in the other seven municipalities, the wheat board price bonus is estimated at $314,000.
I suggest to the committee that a policy which gets results of that kind is not a sound policy; that a policy which gives, unto those who have, still more and gives nothing at all to those who have nothing, is not a sound policy to follow in connection with the marketing of wheat in this country.

Again I say that a system which makes that difference possible in the distribution of funds from the treasury of Canada is not a system that can be advocated or that can be maintained by the federal government.
If I had the time I could give other figures which would further bear out the statement I am now making, but I do not think it necessary to go into all the details; I wish only to give sufficient to justify the government in having come to the conclusion that

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing
there should be some change in policy if we are going to establish a permanent policy for the handling of wheat in Canada. I believe, too, that I have given sufficient to indicate that there should be some change in policy even to establish an emergency procedure which we might follow in years when there are crop failures. It is desired that this emergency policy might, at the same time, relieve us from a considerable number of charges which we have been paying in the past, having to do with the giving of relief in areas where there is no crop.
For some time we have been preparing legislation based upon the policies which we hope to place before this house, and eventually that legislation will be introduced, probably without any considerable delay. But before submitting the legislation or even putting the draft in its final form, I thought it advisable that I should announce to the committee the general policy which the government intends to follow, in order to meet, not only the recommendations which were made by the Turgeon commission which reported at the end of last session, but also, because of experiences we have had during the emergencies we have faced in recent years, and particularly this year, to be in a position to discuss more freely with some of those to whom we have not had access because of lack of announcement of policy down to the present time, the effect of the policy we are announcing on the general marketing of farm products in Canada in future years. In order that this statement may be placed before hon. members in a form which cannot be misunderstood I shall read that statement Of policy and some of the things which led up to it.
Three years ago when we came into office a wheat board had been set up under the Wheat Board Act of 1935. The government was of the opinion that this legislation only provided a means for dealing with an emergency created through the methods followed during previous years in attempting to market Canadian wheat under existing world conditions. It was therefore decided to appoint a royal commission to hold sittings throughout Canada and elsewhere and to report upon past and present methods of marketing wheat as well a3 make recommendations of policy for the future. The commission has reported and recommended the continuance of the open market system, regulation of the grain exchange and encouragement of the pool system of marketing as an alternative to the open market which might be utilized by producers.
Between 1935 and now we have had a continuation of crop failures which has neces-

sitated government assistance. It is now evident that marketing legislation alone will not solve the problems of the wheat growing areas. It is evident that an area which produced the wealth of the period from 1922 to 1928 must be utilized to the fullest possible extent in the effort to develop a nation of home builders.
May I say at this point that as far as the government is concerned we do not feel that the most important thing to be done as a government is to try to see how much wheat we can have produced in Canada. Nor do we think it is important in itself that we should try to have all the cattle produced that can possibly be produced in Canada. Nor do we feel that it is important in itself that we should have all of the dairy products or all the fruit produced in Canada that it is possible to produce. What we think is most important is to put the greatest possible number of families in comfortable circumstances upon the farm lands of this dominion. Believing that, we think that any policy for the marketing of farm products should be based upon the idea that sufficient returns should come to the individual families to make it possible for them to maintain themselves with the ordinary comforts and give proper education to their families. The objective of this government has been and will continue to be to set up as many homes as can possibly be maintained on farms in the prairie section of western Canada. We believe that to do so will assist in solving our labour problem, our railway problem and every other national problem.
May I enlarge on that to say that I am not at all interested in encouraging the production of wheat at thirty-five cents a bushel by putting into operation as many tractors as can possibly be operated on the farm lands of western Canada. Even if it costs forty cents a bushel or if it costs forty-five cents a bushel to grow the same amount of wheat, or a lesser amount, while other products are being produced on the same land, with five families upon, say two and a half sections of land instead of having one family and three tractors and two hired men, then I am in favour of the five families. The encouragement of the placing of more and more families upon our land rather than the production of more and more wheat from our land will assist in solving the labour problem of this country. It will assist also in solving our railway problem to have as many families as possible maintained in comfort upon these lands. It will assist in solving every other national problem which is confronting the

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing
people of Canada at the present time. For that reason I believe that any policy which we follow should be based upon the idea that we want to put families upon the land.. To that end we have already greatly extended and established on a continuing basis the attempt to reestablish farmers in the area where wheat is grown for export. That is, our whole rehabilitation program, which will again receive consideration when our estimates for that purpose come before the house, is directed to the end that more families may be maintained in the area that has been known as the drought area during recent years.
Three years of experience with the Wheat Board Act of 1935 has shown that it is legislation which can only be helpful to deal with a marketing emergency, and could not form the basis for a permanent system of marketing. The present year has shown that it does not provide an equitable method of dealing with the emergency created through drought and grasshoppers. The minimum price per bushel results in those having most receiving most and those having no crop receiving nothing.
Realizing that the present legislation does not offer a solution for our marketing problems and does not provide a means of dealing equitably with the difficulties which stand in the way of home building on the prairies, we intend to introduce legislation which will carry out as far as possible the recommendations of the Turgeon commission, which were:
First, that the government should remain out of the grain trade and our wheat should be marketed by means of the futures market system.
Second, that the grain exchange should be placed under proper supervision.
Third, that encouragement be given to the creation of cooperative marketing associations or pools.
May I repeat that it is our intention to bring down legislation which we hope will make effective all of those recommedations. In addition, we intend to deal by legislation with another phase of the subject which has not been dealt with particularly by the Turgeon commission. We intend to introduce a bill to deal with emergencies, which legislation we hope will make home building on the prairies more secure. This bill will be drafted on the principle that assistance will be given in proportion to need, calculated on an acreage basis, and so adjusted as to encourage home building and maintenance rather than increased wheat production.
In drafting the legislation having to do with the marketing of wheat and for the promotion of cooperatives in relation to marketing of wheat we shall be mindful of the fact that the same principle might be applied to the marketing of other natural products. In other words, we feel that the principle which has been applied to the marketing of wheat during the last three or four years in Canada is not a principle which could be applied to the marketing of other natural products, including other farm products. Therefore we do not think it is a sound principle upon which to base farm product marketing legislation. We cannot agree that there is likely to be permanency to any system of marketing farm products which is based upon price fixing. We prefer to embark upon a policy which will lead to costs of production and standards of product which will invite a paying market for all our farm products.
As I said at the beginning, I wanted to place before the committee, in these general terms, the policy decided upon by the government in order that we might be free, between now and the introduction of the legislation, to discuss it more intelligently with those who will benefit by it. In due course the legislation referred to will be brought in. As I have already said, I make this statement partly because of the request by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar a few nights ago, when my estimates were under consideration, that at the earliest possible date some statement should be made with regard to the policy of the government in relation to wheat; partly because of our desire to be able to discuss the matter more freely both within and without the house and also particularly in order to make known to producers the policy under which we shall probably be operating during the coming crop year. I repeat that when the legislation is under consideration ample opportunity will be given all hon. members to discuss everything I have mentioned to-night, with all the information that is available and all the necessary details with regard to the policies announced in the statement I just made.
I hope the announcement of this decision on the part of the government may have some effect on the discussion of private members' resolutions now on the order paper. It may be that the legislation will be down in any case before those resolutions come up for discussion, but if that should not be the case the business of the house probably would be expedited if those motions could remain in their present position until the legislation is introduced, when we shall have an opportunity to discuss all matters in regard to our

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing
future wheat policy. I wished to place that information on Hansard so that it might be available to all hon. members, and if it meets with the approval of the committee I should like this item to be allowed to stand.

It is all under the Department of Trade and Commerce now?

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: A great many publications dealing with agricultural matters are issued by this department. How many are there, and have there been any new ones this year? What method is employed to acquaint the general public, for whom these publications are intended, as to what ones are available and in what way they are distributed?

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: I could read the list.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: It is not necessary.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext:
I could give some figures to indicate what it amounts to. These are the statistics covering 1937-38, the last year for which I have the figures:
70,166 personal requests received for publications,
630,401 publications mailed on personal requests,
409,199 publications mailed in bulk,
1,727,918 copies of market reports mailed on request,
366,031 copies of press notices,
73,281 clip sheets,
279,620 farm notes,
7,984,764 copies of miscellaneous articles, 10,033 stencils cut for mimeographing,
7,522,131 copies printed from mimeographed stencils
693 jobs on multigraph,
2,320,775 copies printed on multigraph,
2,131,872 envelopes addressed.
Those are the activities in connection with publications in that branch for one year, and they would be approximately the same from year to year.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: But I am asking the minister in what way the public is made acquainted with these publications. How do they learn that the publications are ready, and what they are. They are not sent around indiscriminately. I understand from what the minister has just read that quite a number of them have been asked for. How are the public made acquainted with those publications?

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext:
They are made
acquainted through statements put in the press. Some of these press statements which are issued from time to time are statements indicating to the public that certain publications are available. Then there are certain set lists to which we mail-agricultural col. leges, municipal secretaries, county clerks, members of the House of Commons and of the provincial legislatures, and to some others. Then, they are mailed to persons who may write in. Hon. members will note that 630,000
publications are mailed on personal requests, which means th.ait some interest has been stirred up in relation to them.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: Are not a number of these publications given to the agricultural representatives in the various provinces?

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: Yes, quite a number of them are given to the agricultural representatives. At exhibitions these publications are in the different stands so that people may carry them away or have them explained by the men in attendance.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext:
Does this vote include
any amount for radio advertising?

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: There is no payment for radio services out of this amount. But officials in this branch do prepare the radio statements announced to the public.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: We have found some of the pamphlets very useful, and others not so valuable. In connection with pamphlets dealing with dairy and live stock prices, which are sent to farmers throughout Canada, may I say that I have had letters from farmers stating, " We know from the papers what the price of cattle was last week; what we would like to know and what we would be interested in would be the price of cattle next week or six months from now." So that I suggest there is some wastage in some of the pamphlets sent out. There is a duplication of much of the information which appears in the daily press. Probably it would be better if that money were spent on educational pamphlets, such as were suggested some time ago.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext:
My understanding is
that the reports appearing in the press are supplied by us. We put them in from day to day, across Canada. In addition to that, the daily radio reports are prepared by this department. The report to which the hon. member has referred is a general one which goes out from time to time. Speaking as a practical farmer I would say they are more useful to me than any others because, after all, they show a review of marketing conditions not only on one day but over a period. When one is located, as a good many of us are, two or three hundred miles from where our stock is going to be marketed, it takes us some days to get it to the market place. At the time of shipment we really want to know the market trend. We get as much information out of those mimeographed articles which are sent out as we do from the daily press reports.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: Are all the departmental publications published in French, too?

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: Practically all of them. There may be some that are not, but so far as I know they are practically ail published in that way.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: Is there a substantial demand for them?

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: I understand publicity is given by means of exhibits at the fairs. I have seen some of those exhibits, and I think they are commendable. I would ask the minister, for my own information-and his reply may be of service to others-how a fair makes application for those exhibits, and if any fair, large or small, is entitled to them?

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: The larger fairs are all covered from booths in those fairs where the publications are placed. Individuals in charge of the booths make explanations. As a matter of fact, at the time of the fair in Toronto I had the experience of standing before a booth for fifteen minutes while one of our officials explained to me all about the marketing of hogs. One of the members accompanied me. I must say the official made a very good job of his explanation.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: I heard all about that.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: He convinced me that the publication was a good one. We send men around to the different fairs. We are not able to cover them all, but men are sent to fairs throughout Canada where we do not have booths, but where information in pamphlet form is distributed.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: How would a fair undertake to get an exhibit of this kind? There are a great many small fairs at which exhibits would be of great interest to the farmers. I think education might be promoted in that way as well as any other.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext:
The fair board may
make application for this assistance. We are not able to cover them all, so we select certain groups which cover an area. One year we may select one group and another year another group in the same locality. We try to cover the areas each year, but not always at the same places.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext:
In recent years considerable reorganization has taken place within the department. Frequently, when I am at home,

I find the need of something in the nature of a directory to cover at least the province in which I live. I need something from which I could find out the names of the different officials and where they are located. The telephone book that is issued here forms an excellent directory of the officials in Ottawa, but during the recess I am 3,000 miles away from Ottawa and I need some sort of directory when I want to get in touch with an official in the province.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: As I said to the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) the other evening, that directory has been prepared and is now in the printer's hands. It was impossible to get it out earlier because of this reorganization. We wanted to have the staffs complete so that the directory would be up to date.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: Will that directory cover all the provinces?

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: All the services and all the provinces.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: Who will get copies? Will it be advertised in the press?

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: Anyone who desires will be able to get it by writing in. We will probably send it to all hon. members, and in any case it will be mailed out to those on our mailing list.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: No doubt there is a great deal of useful information in these pamphlets, but many people do not know where to get them. I have been asked several times where such and such a pamphlet could be got. A person might see one in an office or in someone else's home and want to know where to get it. The system of distributing seems to be lacking in some way. Possibly this directory will help considerably because it will enable the rural people to know where to get it.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext:
Has the minister
thought of putting a list of these valuable pamphlets in the post offices? Possibly a card could be prepared with the names of the most important pamphlets.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext:
I think something along that line might be done and I shall give consideration to it. I may say that different plans have been tried out in the department at different times. We have tried putting the pamphlets into banks, post offices and other _ places where they would be available, but there has always been a great wastage in that method. We find that it does not pay to make bulk distributions at different points.

Supply-Agriculture-Publicity
We get better results by trying to advertise the fact that pamphlets are available, and then those who really want them can write in. Much of the information gets about, not directly from a pamphlet but from someone who has read a pamphlet and tells others about it.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: To what extent are these distributed through the schools?

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: They are not distributed through the schools except where a teacher writes in for them and asks for copies to be used in connection with teaching agriculture in the school.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: I do not know whether the expense would be prohibitive, but I was thinking of an inexpensive cabinet with a glass front which could be placed in the important post offices. This cabinet would contain a complete set of the most important pamphlets, and would bear a notice to the effect that copies could be obtained by writing to such and such an address. I have thought a number of times that it was really too bad that valuable pamphlets like these, are not more widely known. As hon. members said a minute-ago, many people do not know that these pamphlets exist or where to get them. The material contained in them is incomparably valuable for men doing practical work.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: Has the minister any idea of the extent to which teachers apply for these pamphlets?

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS

There are certain special types of pamphlets for which a considerable number of teachers apply. These are pamphlets that will ,be helpful in teaching agriculture, but generally speaking there is no application for a great mass of the pamphlets.
Mr. COLDWrELL: I know from personal experience that many of these pamphlets have proved most valuable in the schools, and to the communities through the schools. I was wondering if some effort could not be made to have the provincial departments of education or the normal schools direct attention to these pamphlets. This would save the department sending them out. I may say that I knew nothing of these pamphlets when I started to teach, and it was only by accident that I got a list of them. I sent for some of the pamphlets, and I believe I am still on the mailing list of the department.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext:
Speaking as a practical teacher and principal of a good many years experience, I think something could be done along the lines of preparing a circular to send
out from time to time to every rural school in the west, either through the provincial departments or direct from Ottawa.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: I am not familiar with what is done in all the schools, but when I was minister of education in Saskatchewan the practice in the normal school was to send for pamphlets to all the dominions. You can go into the normal library in Regina and see copies of pamphlets describing conditions in Australia, New Zealand and so on. I expect that this would be generally the practice in all normal schools across the continent. The teachers who are taking courses in these normal schools have the opportunity of learning about these pamphlets, and I would expect that when most of them go out to teach they would make use of them.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: I believe in recent years certain courses of study have referred to certain of the pamphlets of the Department of Agriculture.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: The hon. gentlemen to my left who have just spoken come from Saskatchewan and Alberta. I may tell them that for many years in Manitoba these publications have been noted in the departmental journal and in the journal of the teachers' federation. As the minister has said, teachers in training in the normal school have been made aware of these publications. I do not know what happens in Saskatchewan or Alberta, but I know that has been the case in Manitoba for a great number of years.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: There is a practice in China whereby a rich man pays his doctor just as long as he is well. When he is sick he does not pay. There are doctors of every description in the Department of Agriculture. I suggest that they receive salaries only when things are good for the farmers. When the farmers have any reason to complain, all the doctors in the Department of Agriculture should not receive one cent of salary.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: What about the lawyers?

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: There are no lawyers in that department.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext:
It has been intimated
that the people of Alberta would not know anything about these pamphlets, but I must tell hon. members that the department of education in that province has always kept these pamphlets before the people all the time. The endeavour has been to heal the sick, and, if possible, to have no sick, so far as the knowledge distributed from this department is concerned. I am sure that we in

speechtext: There is a pamphlet known as Economic Annalist. I do not know if it is issued by this department or not, but if so, I would ask the minister if he is responsible for the opinions therein expressed, or if he knows just what those opinions are.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: Will the minister give us a brief explanation of the work that is done in connection with these first four items?

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext:
The imperial agricultural bureaux were set up as a result of the imperial agricultural research conference of 1927, which recommended that eight bureaux be established to collect, collate and disseminate information on research in selected branches of agricultural science, and generally to assist research workers in the empire with information on their subjects and with introductions to other research workers.
These proposals were accepted by empire governments, and in 1928 a number of these bureaux were set up. Since 1929 this service of common empire interest has been maintained from a fund jointly subscribed by the governments of the empire and administered by an executive council, composed of representatives directly appointed by the governments for that purpose. The functions of the bureaux have to do with the distribution of information; they do not themselves undertake research, but they gather and make available to every country that is a member of the bureaux the results of the research work carried on.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: What is the work undertaken at the Farnham laboratory, and where is it located?

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: Parasitology is undertaken at that laboratory. It is at Farnham, in England.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: Is this a grant, and have we a representative on the bureaux?

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: It is a grant made to these bureaux, and from them we get the information.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext:
Have we Canadian
representatives on the various bureaux?

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext:

Supply-Agriculture-Animal Pathology

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS

Has the minister any
idea of the total amount expended by the imperial government and charged to the other dominions?

amount, but each part of the empire contributes its just share in proportion to its agricultural activities.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS

private individuals could have soils analyzed free of charge, and how they would go about having this done.

speechtext: There are local laboratories, some of them provincial and some operating with our assistance, and people can send in soils and have them analyzed. maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OF OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OF FISH IN STREAMS
